DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
The core idea of this proposal is reasonable. Harbourside is clearly priced below its competitors, and there is probably room to raise rates. The problem is the evidence. The hotel's room count is wrong in the revenue calculation. The "direct test" of price sensitivity is confused by the strongest season of the year. And the two-night minimum conflicts with the hotel's largest source of Saturday bookings. As a result, £204,000 is not a floor. It is an upper estimate built on optimistic assumptions.

## 1. The revenue calculation uses the wrong number of rooms

Section 2 says Harbourside is a **112-room** hotel. Section 5 calculates revenue across **124 rooms**.

- With 124 rooms: 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ **£203,800**, which is the figure in the proposal.
- With 112 rooms: 112 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ **£184,000**.

This mistake alone overstates the gain by about **£20,000 a year**.

## 2. Not every occupied room pays the BAR

The calculation applies the £20 rise to every occupied weekend room. Several kinds of booking won't pay it:

- **Corporate and contracted group rates**, which the proposal says will be honoured (section 6).
- **Wedding blocks** booked through couples. These make up about **38% of Saturday bookings** (section 4) and are typically sold at group rates.
- **OTA bookings**, where commission (often 15–20%) takes part of any rate rise.
- **Reservations already made** for June onwards at £145. This means the first year's gain would be smaller still.

If even a third of weekend room-nights fall outside the BAR, the realistic gain drops to roughly **£120,000–£130,000**. The proposal needs the actual BAR share of weekend room-nights to estimate this properly.

## 3. The "direct test" of price sensitivity is confused by the season

The rate rose from £135 to £145 in the last week of June 2025, and July occupancy then rose from 81% to 89%. But Table 1 and section 2 show why July would have risen anyway:

- July and August are the strongest months, "driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays."
- Occupancy kept climbing to **93% in August**, then gradually fell back. This is a normal seasonal pattern.
- June's 81% was itself a dip from May's 85%, and it happened *before* the price rise.

The comparison shows the seasonal pattern, not the effect of the price change. A useful test would compare July–December 2025 with the same months of 2024, or with how competitors performed over the same period. The claim that the higher rate "reinforced our positioning" is speculation.

## 4. The value-for-money score would be affected by the change

A value-for-money score of 8.4 measures how guests feel about paying **£145**. Part of the reason the score is high is that the hotel is £20–£35 cheaper than its competitors. A rise to £165 would put Harbourside level with the cheapest competitor, so this score will probably fall. It is not evidence that the higher rate will be accepted.

## 5. The two-night minimum may cost money, not just add unquantified revenue

Section 4 has two facts that work against the proposal:

- Wedding guests make up about 38% of Saturday bookings, and they "arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning." Those are single-night stays.
- A two-night minimum would require these guests to pay for a night they don't want, or send them to other hotels. It could also strain the relationship with Quayside Hall.

More generally:

- The hotel sold out **31 Saturdays** in 2025. On the roughly **21 Saturdays it didn't sell out**, a minimum stay simply turns away single-night guests the hotel has room for.
- Minimum stays usually work as a **date-specific tool**, used only on high-demand dates. A blanket rule is likely to lose revenue on quieter weekends.

Calling the minimum stay a pure upside that "puts no value" on itself is therefore misleading. It could easily have a **negative** effect. At the least, wedding blocks should be exempt and the rule applied only to dates that are forecast to sell out.

## 6. "Floor rather than target" isn't justified

The estimate assumes occupancy holds at 2025 levels. That isn't conservative; it is the central assumption, and the evidence for it is the confused test in point 3. A fairer way to present it is a **breakeven point**: at £165, weekend occupancy could fall from 79% to about **69%** before room revenue drops below the £145 baseline. That is a reasonable cushion, and a more honest way to describe the risk than calling the figure a floor.

## What holds up

- The competitor comparison is correct. £145 is £20–£35 below a £165–£180 range, and £165 would put the hotel at the bottom of that range.
- The 2025 average of 79% is correct (950 ÷ 12 = 79.2%).
- The arithmetic is correct for the inputs used.
- The weekly pick-up review against the same weeks of 2025 is a sensible way to monitor the change.

## Smaller points

- **The monitoring trigger is slow.** A five-point monthly fall shows up only after the month ends. Weekly booking pace, which section 6 already tracks, should be the trigger.
- **The June 2025 baseline mixes two rates.** The price changed in the last week of June, so that month was mostly at £135.
- **"Recovered strongly since 2023"** is stated without any supporting data.

## Suggested revisions

1. **Correct the room count to 112**, and base the uplift on BAR room-nights only, net of OTA commission.
2. **Replace the June-to-July comparison** with a same-month comparison against 2024, or against competitors.
3. **Restrict the two-night minimum** to forecast high-demand Saturdays, and exempt wedding and group blocks.
4. **Present the revenue as a range with a breakeven occupancy**, not as a floor.
5. **Show the first-year figure separately**, starting from 1 June and allowing for bookings already made.

A rate rise to £165 may still be the right decision. But the case for it rests on a wrong room count and a misread seasonal pattern, and the minimum-stay part of the proposal could undo some of the gain.
